client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time I try to sit down and focus on work, these memories of her just flood in and I can't concentrate on anything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly — it feels like nothing can really change the fact that she's gone.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds incredibly heavy — losing your grandmother, and then having her memory surface just when you're trying to hold things together, is a really painful kind of grief. Your voice carries a quiet exhaustion, like you're speaking from a place of deep hurt rather than despair, and that makes complete sense given what you've been through. While nothing we do here will change the reality of her passing, what we *can* work on together is helping you find a way to hold that grief without it feeling like it's swallowing you whole — and that's a meaningful change worth exploring.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess that's a fair way to put it — "swallowing me whole" is actually kind of exactly what it feels like. But I'm not sure how you "hold" grief differently, like what does that even mean in practice? It sounds nice in theory, but when I'm sitting at my desk and a memory just hits me out of nowhere, I don't really know what I'm supposed to do with that.
therapist: That's such a fair and grounding question — and the way you're asking it, with a kind of quiet urgency, tells me you genuinely want something real and practical, not just comforting words. One concrete place to start is this: when a memory hits you at your desk, instead of fighting it or pushing through, you might try pausing for just 30 seconds to simply *name* what's happening — "I'm missing her right now" — which helps your brain shift from being overwhelmed *by* the feeling to gently *observing* it. It won't make the memory hurt less, but it can create just enough space that you're not completely swept away, and over time that small act of acknowledgment can make the waves feel a little less sudden.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of tightness — really reflects how much pressure you're holding right now, like you're already bracing against the possibility of losing control. That fear makes complete sense, and I want to gently offer a different way to look at it: the lid you're keeping on things isn't actually preventing the grief from affecting your work — those flooding memories are already breaking through, which suggests the strategy of containment may be costing you more energy than it's saving. What if naming it briefly isn't opening a floodgate, but actually giving the feeling just enough acknowledgment that it doesn't have to keep knocking so loudly to get your attention?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually... makes a weird kind of sense, and I hate that it does, because it means the thing I've been doing to cope might be making it worse. I don't really trust myself to be able to stop once I start feeling it.
therapist: The way you said that — softly, quickly, with a kind of held-breath quality — tells me this fear of losing control feels very real and close to the surface right now, even as part of you is starting to see things differently. That fear makes so much sense, but I'd gently invite you to examine the evidence: in all the times grief has hit you unexpectedly this past month, have you actually fallen apart beyond recovery, or have you — even painfully — always found your way back? Building in a small "exit ramp" can help too, like deciding in advance that after you name it, you'll take three slow breaths and return to one specific task, giving yourself a concrete path back rather than trusting an open-ended process.

client: When you put it that way, I have to admit that I haven't actually completely fallen apart — I've cried a few times, but I always did eventually get up and keep going. I guess I've been so focused on the fear of losing control that I forgot to notice I've actually been surviving it. therapist: There's something really significant in what you just recognized — that despite everything, you have always gotten back up — and even though your voice carries a kind of breathless nervousness, like part of you is still catching up to that realization, it's worth pausing to let that sink in: you have evidence that you're more resilient than your fear has been telling you. On the practical side, the suddenness of grief memories is real, which is why it can help to practice the "name it + exit ramp" sequence *before* you need it — even just rehearsing it once today when you're calm, so it becomes a familiar path your mind can find more automatically when things get hard. You're already doing more than you've been giving yourself credit for.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Practicing it when I'm calm actually sounds more manageable than trying to figure it out in the middle of a wave — I hadn't thought about it that way. I think I can try that today, maybe just once, quietly to myself. But I'll be honest, there's still this part of me that feels almost guilty for trying to "manage" the grief, like if I get better at handling it, it means I'm somehow moving on from her or caring less.
therapist: The way you said that — quickly, with a kind of high, tight quality in your voice — feels like someone trying to hold something tender very carefully, and that guilt you're describing is one of the most common and painful parts of grief. But I'd gently offer this reframe: learning to carry grief without being crushed by it isn't a sign that she mattered less — it's actually something she would likely have *wanted* for you, and your love for her lives in your memories, your values, the way she shaped you, none of which gets smaller just because you learn to breathe again. Getting better at handling grief isn't moving on *from* her; it's finding a way to move forward *with* her.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
